title: Method and code
intro: This page explains the methods behind the research pages and gives the code to run the same analyses on your own data, location and question. Our Sisal results are one example of each analysis.

sections.title: Ecosystem analysis
datasets: Landsat 5 TM, 7 ETM+, 8 and 9 OLI, Collection 2 Tier 1 Level-2 (surface reflectance), via Google Earth Engine
Global Mangrove Watch: used for the first mangrove mask, to select the points. The final mangrove map is based on NDVI, so Global Mangrove Watch is not the definitive mask.
Sentinel-2 SR Harmonized: only the background image of the map (January–May 2024). Not used for NDVI, because its record is too short to detect tipping points and early warning signals.

useCases.title: NDVI time series for your location
useCases.howMade: Monthly maximum NDVI from Landsat (1993–2026) for 1138 random points in the Sisal area. Each series is regularised to monthly values, deseasonalised and detrended (STL), and corrected for the upward drift caused by the growing number of images per year. On these series we (1) detect breakpoints, (2) test for early warning signals before each loss, and (3) group all points into shape classes, shown on the map.
keyChoices: Monthly maximum NDVI: the maximum limits the effect of clouds; monthly steps are fine enough not to miss tipping points, which develop over several months.
Data from 1993 onwards: before that there are fewer than 12 Landsat images per year over Sisal.
The number of images per year increases over time, which pushes the monthly maximum upwards; this drift is removed in the detrending.
Landsat and Sentinel-2 are not merged, because of sensor differences.
whatYouNeed: A free Google Earth Engine account. Python 3 with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels (STL) and scipy (Kendall's tau and smoothing).
steps: Open the Earth Engine script in the Earth Engine Code Editor. Choose one location, or upload a CSV with the coordinates of several points.
Run the script and export the monthly maximum NDVI per point as a CSV to Google Drive.
Download the CSV from Google Drive to your computer.
Open the notebook, set the path to your CSV and run all cells.
The notebook regularises, deseasonalises and detrends each series and saves one plot per point, like the plots on the Ecosystem page.

useCases.title: Tipping point analysis for your own location
keyChoices: Breakpoint: a change of at least 0.25 NDVI within 12 months, after which the new level persists for at least 2 years. A drop followed by a quick recovery is resilience, not a breakpoint.
whatYouNeed: A free Google Earth Engine account. Python 3 with pandas, numpy, matplotlib and statsmodels (STL).
steps: Make the NDVI time series as in the example "NDVI time series for your location".
Run the breakpoint detection in the notebook: a change of at least 0.25 NDVI within 12 months, after which the new level persists for at least 2 years.
It lists every point with a breakpoint, with its date and magnitude, and marks it in the plot.

useCases.title: Early warning signals for your own location
keyChoices: Early warning signals are computed only on the deseasonalised NDVI before the start of each loss, because an abrupt drop inside the rolling window would create false increases in variance and autocorrelation.
The significance of the early warning signals is tested against AR(1) surrogates; points without a breakpoint serve as controls.
whatYouNeed: A free Google Earth Engine account. Python 3 with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels (STL) and scipy (Kendall's tau and smoothing).
steps: Find the breakpoints as in the example "Tipping point analysis for your own location".
For each point with a loss, take the deseasonalised NDVI before the start of the loss (at least 5 years needed).
Detrend it and compute the rolling standard deviation, AR1, kurtosis and skewness, with Kendall's tau per metric.
Test the significance against AR(1) surrogates and compare with control points without a breakpoint.
Place each point in the scenario matrix and check the sensitivity to window size and bandwidth.

useCases.title: Shape-class map of your area

keyChoices.text: Shape classes are based on the net NDVI change and the turnover of each series, with fixed thresholds.
keyChoices.more: The start and end level are the median of the first and last 3 years. Loss: net change of −0.3 or less. Gain: net change of +0.3 or more. Loss + recovery: mangrove (NDVI 0.3 or more) at the start and the end, but below 0.3 for at least 2 years in between. High turnover: turnover of 1.4 or more, a whole year below NDVI 0.25, or a monthly trend below 0. Non-mangrove: below 0.3 at the start and the end, with a mean NDVI below 0.25. All other points are stable.

whatYouNeed: A free Google Earth Engine account. Python 3 with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, statsmodels (STL) and scipy (Kendall's tau and smoothing).
steps: Make the NDVI time series as in the example "NDVI time series for your location", for many random points in your area.
In the notebook, compute the net NDVI change and turnover per point and assign the shape classes (stable, gain, loss, loss + recovery, high turnover, non-mangrove).
Plot the classes on a map using the point coordinates.

routes.title: Quick (Global Mangrove Watch)
routes.description: Works anywhere and needs nothing to prepare. About 1–2 hours, mostly waiting for exports. Coarser.
steps: Create a free Earth Engine account and a non-commercial Cloud project.
Make scripts 1, 2 and 3 in the Code Editor and set MY_ASSETS and NAME at the top of each.
Test on Sisal first (draw nothing), then draw your own area.
Run script 1 and start the export in Tasks; wait.
Run script 2 with MASK_SOURCE = 'GMW' and export; wait.
Run script 3: map, legend and areas.

routes.title: Accurate (training points, our method)
routes.description: Mexico via CONABIO, or anywhere with your own points. About 2–3 hours. Best accuracy.
steps: Create a free Earth Engine account and a non-commercial Cloud project.
Make scripts 1, 2a, 2 and 3 in the Code Editor and set MY_ASSETS and NAME at the top of each.
Test on Sisal first (draw nothing), then draw your own area.
Run script 1 and start the export in Tasks; wait.

Download the CONABIO land-use maps of your area (or prepare your own points CSV). Clip each map to your study area first, in Mapshaper or QGIS: the Mexico files are too big to upload to Earth Engine. Then upload the clipped files to your assets.
Run script 2a to make the training points, and export.
Run script 2 with MASK_SOURCE = 'POINTS' and export; wait.
Run script 3: map, legend and areas.

sections.title: Climatology analysis
datasets: ERA5-Land, land cell: air temperature (daily maximum and minimum), rainfall. Daily, {record.airTemperature.start} to {record.airTemperature.end}.
ERA5, sea cell: wind speed, wave height, wave direction, sea surface temperature. Daily, {record.windSpeed.start} to {record.windSpeed.end}.
Satellite altimetry: sea level. Monthly, {record.seaLevel.start} to {record.seaLevel.end}.
HURDAT2 (NOAA National Hurricane Center): storm tracks. Every 6 hours, {storms.start} to {storms.end}.
limitations: One grid cell per variable, not an area average; reanalysis (model) data, not local measurements.
The record periods differ per variable; salinity only covers {record.salinity.start} to {record.salinity.end}, so later storms have no salinity.
Too few storms ({storms.total} in {storms.start} to {storms.end}) for a trend test.

useCases.title: Storm tracks near a location
useCases.howMade: We study {storms.studied} storms in detail: all passed within 100 km of Sisal and have daily climate data (ERA5 starts in {record.windSpeed.start}; earlier storms are counted, not studied). {storms.notCounted} are studied but not counted: near Sisal they were weaker than tropical storm strength.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show the tracks of the storms that came within 100 km of Sisal, coloured by strength, and to see where they come from.
whatYouNeed: The HURDAT2 text file of your ocean from the National Hurricane Center (Atlantic, or North-East Pacific for the Pacific coast of Mexico and Central America).
The latitude and longitude of your location, a radius in km and a minimum wind. The coastlines of the world are included in the package.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Download the HURDAT2 file of your ocean from nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat and put it in the example_data folder.
Open storm_tracks.py and set the file, the name and coordinates of your location, the radius, the minimum wind, the years and the size of the map.
Run python storm_tracks.py and read the list of storms it prints.
Open the map (PNG) and the storm lists (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Events per month and year
useCases.howMade: Counted are tropical and subtropical storms of at least tropical-storm strength within 100 km of Sisal, {storms.start} to {storms.end}. This gives {storms.total} storms.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to count the storms that came within 100 km of Sisal per month and per year, 1950 to 2024, and to see when in the year storms come.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with one row per event and the columns name and date (YYYY-MM-DD), and the first and last year of your record.
No list of events? For storms, the helper script makes one for any location, radius and minimum wind from the HURDAT2 tracks of the National Hurricane Center (Atlantic and North-East Pacific).
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.

Storms: download the HURDAT2 file of your ocean, open make_events_from_hurdat2.py, set the file, your location, the radius, the minimum wind and the years, and run it. Other events: write your own CSV with name and date.
Open event_counts.py and set the CSV path, what the events are called, the place and the first and last year of the record.
Run python event_counts.py and read the checks it prints.
Open the chart (PNG) and the counts per month and per year (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Anomaly chart around an event
useCases.howMade: An anomaly is a daily value minus the mean of the same calendar day (baseline: {storms.baseline}). The charts show {storms.windowDays} days around the peak date; the box is the storm period and the dashed line the day the storm was closest to Sisal.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show how air temperature, wind, waves, rainfall and sea surface temperature at Sisal differed from normal around each of the studied storms.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with a date column (YYYY-MM-DD) and one numeric column per variable, with at least 10 years of daily data.
No own data? The helper script exports daily ERA5-Land data (air temperature, rainfall, wind) for any coordinates from Google Earth Engine.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Put your data in a CSV file in the input format, or export it with get_era5_point.js in the Earth Engine Code Editor.
Open event_anomaly.py and set the CSV path, the event name and dates, the days before and after, and the baseline.
Run python event_anomaly.py and read the data checks it prints.
Open the chart (PNG) and the anomaly values (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Wave and wind rose
useCases.howMade: The compass has 8 sectors of 45°, and each day is counted in the sector the waves come from, {wave.start} to {wave.end}. The wide wedge is all {wave.all} days, the narrow wedge the {wave.storm} rough-sea days with waves above {wave.threshold} m.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show from which directions the waves come at Sisal, on all days and on rough-sea days with waves above 2 m.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with a date column (YYYY-MM-DD), a column with the direction in degrees (0 to 360, the direction it comes from) and a column to decide which days count, for example wave height or wind speed. At least 10 years of daily data.
No own data? The helper script of the anomaly chart exports daily ERA5-Land data for any coordinates from Google Earth Engine; wave data comes from the Copernicus Climate Data Store.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Put your data in a CSV file in the input format.
Open wave_wind_rose.py and set the CSV path, the direction column, the column and threshold for the rough days, and the names for the chart.
Run python wave_wind_rose.py and read the data checks and the table of percentages it prints.
Open the rose (PNG) and the numbers per sector (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Seasonal cycle
useCases.howMade: For each calendar month the line is the mean of all daily values of the record and the band runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile. Rainfall is the mean monthly total and sea level has no band.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show what a typical year looks like at Sisal for air temperature, rainfall, wind, waves, sea surface temperature and salinity.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with a date column (YYYY-MM-DD) and one numeric column per variable, with at least 10 years of daily data.
No own data? The helper script of the anomaly chart exports daily ERA5-Land data (air temperature, rainfall, wind) for any coordinates from Google Earth Engine.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Put your data in a CSV file in the input format.
Open seasonal_cycle.py and set the CSV path and, per column, its name, unit and "mean" (line with band) or "total" (monthly total, for rainfall).
Run python seasonal_cycle.py and read the data checks it prints.
Open the chart (PNG) and the monthly numbers (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Long-term trend with significance
useCases.howMade: Annual means over the record of each variable (years with at least 90% of the days), with a linear trend per decade (sea level: per year). The trend line is drawn only when p < {trend.pLimit}.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show how air temperature, rainfall, wind, waves, sea surface temperature and salinity at Sisal changed over the years, and whether the trend is significant.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with a date column (YYYY-MM-DD) and one numeric column per variable, with at least 20 years of daily data (10 complete years is the minimum for a rough picture).
No own data? The helper script of the anomaly chart exports daily ERA5-Land data (air temperature, rainfall, wind) for any coordinates from Google Earth Engine.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, scipy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Put your data in a CSV file in the input format.
Open long_term_trend.py and set the CSV path and, per column, its name and unit.
Run python long_term_trend.py and read the data checks and the trends it prints.
Open the chart (PNG) and the annual means and trends (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

useCases.title: Monthly range and running mean
useCases.howMade: Per month the band runs from the lowest to the highest daily value, and the line is the 365-day running mean. Sea level shows the monthly anomaly and its 12-month running mean, with trends for {seaLevel.periods}.
useCases.howWeUsed: We used it to show, for air temperature, rainfall, wind, waves, sea surface temperature and salinity at Sisal, how far each month ranged and how the level changed slowly over the years.
whatYouNeed: A CSV file with a date column (YYYY-MM-DD) and one numeric column per variable, with at least 10 years of daily data (a running mean needs a record of more than one year).
No own data? The helper script of the anomaly chart exports daily ERA5-Land data (air temperature, rainfall, wind) for any coordinates from Google Earth Engine.
steps: Install Python and the packages in requirements.txt (pandas, numpy, matplotlib) in a virtual environment.
Put your data in a CSV file in the input format.
Open monthly_range.py and set the CSV path and, per column, its name and unit.
Run python monthly_range.py and read the data checks it prints.
Open the chart (PNG) and the monthly numbers (CSV) in the output folder, and check the warnings before you use them.

sections.title: Stakeholder mapping
sections.galleryHint: Methods you can use with people in your own area. Pick one to see how it works and what you need.
datasets: Interviews with seven stakeholders in Sisal, September and October 2026: semi-structured, held in Spanish with translation support, recorded and transcribed.
Stakeholder types, each shown only by a code: academic (AC), community restoration group (CR), conservation NGO (NGO), eco-tourism (ET), government (GOV).
Areas drawn by the stakeholders on a map during the interview (question 5), then placed on the Sentinel-2 base map (January–May 2024).
limitations: Seven stakeholders, so it does not represent the whole community.
Areas are approximate: they show where people meant, not exact boundaries.
Periods come from memory; vague periods ("recent", "over 30 years") are shown as approximate on the timeline.

Interviews went through translation, so the format was mostly question and answer, with few follow-up questions. Statements are paraphrased in English from the translated transcripts; hearsay is marked as such.

useCases.title: Map interview
useCases.howMade: A semi-structured interview in four parts: general, mangrove change and its drivers, communication, and the present and future. Question 5 is the mapping step: the stakeholder draws the areas that changed most on a map and explains what caused each change. Interviews are recorded and transcribed. Each stakeholder type also gets a short module with its own questions (developers, eco-tourism, fishers, government, residents, researchers).
useCases.howWeUsed: We interviewed seven stakeholders in Sisal in September and October 2026. Questions 2 to 5 (change, causes, sudden events and the map) are the basis of the three themes on the Stakeholders page.
useCases.howWeUsedLinkLabel: See it on the Stakeholders page
whatYouNeed: The interview guide and consent form, a printed map of your area for question 5, a recorder, and an interpreter if you don't speak the local language.
steps: Print a map of your area for the drawing question, or export one with the Sentinel-2 script from the Ecosystem method.
Read the consent form together and ask for the three consents (recording, use of answers and drawings, data storage). Give the stakeholder a code: type + number, for example NGO1.
Ask the general questions, then the questions on change and drivers, and add the module for this stakeholder type.
At question 5, let the stakeholder draw and number each area. Ask when it changed and why, per area.
Transcribe the recording, photograph the map, and store names and recordings separately from the codes.

useCases.title: From interview to table
useCases.howMade: Every statement is sorted into one of three themes (extent, condition, disturbance and recovery) and written as one row: area number, zone, change, period, start and end year, certainty, cause, stakeholder code and type, and a paraphrase in English.
useCases.howWeUsed: The three themes on the Stakeholders page, with one quote per stakeholder per area.
useCases.howWeUsedLinkLabel: See it on the Stakeholders page
whatYouNeed: The transcripts and photographed maps from the map interview, and a spreadsheet program.
steps: Open coding_sheet_template.csv.
Sort each statement into extent, condition, or disturbance and recovery (see theme_rules.md).
Write one row per area per stakeholder. The paraphrase gives their view in their words, not your interpretation.
Turn the period into a start and end year, and mark it exact, approximate, ongoing or expected (see theme_rules.md).
Check every row for names and personal details, and remove them.
